issues.legal_issue: Criminal proceedings arising from a private landlord-tenant dispute that the parties voluntarily settled may be quashed where continuation would be futile.
material_facts: The incident arose during renovation work at a property where one family occupied part of the property as tenants, and the dispute was essentially between the landlord and tenant families.

The informant and the alleged injured persons signed a compromise stating that the dispute had been settled voluntarily and that they were willing to compound the criminal case and a related complaint.
The informant affirmed the compromise before the High Court, and the accused paid money to the complainants under the settlement.
The FIR was lodged 19 days after the incident, and the accused had also filed a counter-complaint.
The High Court found that the underlying dispute had been settled and that continuing the criminal proceedings would be futile.
issues.conclusion: The High Court properly exercised its inherent power to quash the proceedings, and the Supreme Court found no error warranting interference.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court may quash criminal proceedings in light of a settlement when, considering the nature and circumstances of the dispute, continuation of the proceedings would be futile. The High Court considered the guiding principles in Gian Singh v. State of Punjab and Narinder Singh v. State of Punjab; the Supreme Court upheld its application of those principles to this essentially landlord-tenant dispute and the parties’ compromise.

rule.if: criminal_quashing_proceeding and private_landlord_tenant_dispute and voluntary_compromise_executed and complainant_affirmed_compromise and continuation_would_be_futile

predicates.criminal_quashing_proceeding: A party asks a court to quash criminal proceedings arising from an alleged incident.
predicates.private_landlord_tenant_dispute: The alleged criminal incident arose from a private dispute essentially between landlord and tenant families.
predicates.voluntary_compromise_executed: The parties executed a compromise stating that they had settled the dispute voluntarily.
predicates.complainant_affirmed_compromise: The complainant affirmed the compromise before the court considering the quashing request.
predicates.continuation_would_be_futile: The circumstances show that continuing the criminal proceedings would serve no useful purpose.

issues.definition: When a criminal quashing proceeding concerns a private landlord-tenant dispute, the parties voluntarily executed a compromise, the complainant affirmed it, and continuation would be futile, the criminal proceedings may be quashed.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a separate hearing for injured persons does not warrant appellate interference with a quashing order when they signed the compromise and one of them appeared before the court that made the order.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that they were injured persons who had not been made parties to, or heard in, the High Court proceedings.
The compromise deed was signed by the informant and the appellants, and the appellants did not dispute that it had been executed.
One appellant was present before the High Court and appeared as counsel for the informant.
The informant affirmed the compromise before the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The appellants’ complaint that they had not been heard did not provide a basis for interfering with the High Court’s quashing order.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court assessed the claimed lack of notice in light of the record showing that the alleged injured persons had signed the compromise, had not disputed its execution, and that one appellant was present before the High Court. In those circumstances, the complaint did not establish a reason to interfere with the quashing order.

rule.if: appeal_against_quashing_order and injured_appellants_not_separately_heard and injured_appellants_signed_compromise and one_injured_appellant_was_present and compromise_execution_not_disputed

predicates.appeal_against_quashing_order: An appeal challenges an order quashing criminal proceedings.
predicates.injured_appellants_not_separately_heard: Persons claiming to have been injured were not separately made parties to or heard in the proceeding that resulted in quashing.
predicates.injured_appellants_signed_compromise: The persons claiming to have been injured signed the compromise concerning the dispute.
predicates.one_injured_appellant_was_present: One person claiming to have been injured was present before the court that quashed the proceedings.
predicates.compromise_execution_not_disputed: The persons challenging the quashing order did not dispute that the compromise had been executed.
predicates.no_appellate_interference_for_lack_of_he: The appellate court does not interfere with the quashing order on the ground that the injured persons were not separately heard.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a quashing order, injured appellants were not separately heard but signed the compromise, one was present before the quashing court, and execution of the compromise is undisputed, the lack of a separate hearing does not warrant appellate interference.
